input.question: If the Hubble telescope can zoom into the far reaches of the galaxy, why can't we just point it at Earth-like planets to see if they have water/vegetation etc.
input.ground_truth: We can't "see" earth like planets. They are too far away. The hubble telescope is great for seeing faint and far away things. We can see faint stars. We can see distant galaxies. We can see BOTH of these things because they give off light. We point our telescope at these and basically "leave the shutter open". This gathers light over an extended period of time. **Planets do not give off light. They only reflect light. This is not enough light to actually "see" the planet itself.** And on the remote chance we do see it, it isn't in enough detail to see the surface. The reason we know planets exist is not because we "see" them. It is because we see the effect they have on the stars they orbit.

response.prediction:
Okay! Imagine the Hubble telescope is like a really big pair of binoculars, but even stronger. It can look super far away and see tiny, tiny dots that are actually other galaxies or stars.

But here’s the thing: when Hubble looks at something super far away, those things look like tiny, tiny dots—like a little speck of dust. Now, if we want to look at a planet that’s like Earth, but far away, it’s like trying to see a tiny marble next to a big lamp from across the whole soccer field at night. The marble is so, so small and not very bright by itself.

Also, the Earth-like planet is super duper far away. When Hubble looks at it, it can’t see any details like water or trees or grass. It just sees a little dot. It’s like trying to see the grass in your backyard from space—it just looks like a green blob, not individual blades of grass.

We need even bigger and better telescopes, or special tricks, to see those tiny details on faraway planets. Right now, Hubble just isn’t strong enough to see if those planets have water or plants. But scientists are working on new ways to do that!
